expected_claims: NIST stands for National Institute of Standards and Technology.
The document is a cross-sectoral companion resource for the AI RMF focused on generative AI risks and suggested actions.
The AI RMF is voluntary and helps organizations incorporate trustworthiness considerations and manage AI risks.
Generative AI models emulate input-data structure and characteristics to produce derived synthetic content.
Governance, Content Provenance, Pre-Deployment Testing, and Incident Disclosure are the four primary considerations.
Risk is the composite of an event's likelihood and the magnitude of its consequences.
Confabulation is confidently stated erroneous or false content, also described as hallucination or fabrication.
Data privacy risk includes leakage, unauthorized use, disclosure, or de-anonymization of sensitive or personally identifiable data.
The risk covers amplified biases, subgroup performance disparities, discrimination, and undesirable output homogeneity.
Training and operating GAI can use substantial resources and have energy, carbon, and environmental footprints.
Human-AI configuration can lead to anthropomorphization, automation bias, over-reliance, aversion, or emotional entanglement.
High-integrity information distinguishes fact, fiction, opinion, and inference; acknowledges uncertainty; and is transparent, verifiable, and linked to evidence.
The risk is eased access to or synthesis of dangerous CBRN information or design capabilities.
Third-party datasets, models, and libraries can be improperly obtained or insufficiently vetted, reducing transparency and accountability.
GAI can ease unauthorized replication of copyrighted, trademarked, or licensed content and can create copyright concerns through memorization.
Organizations can revise risk tiers, governance regimes, oversight, human review, tracking, documentation, and management oversight for GAI.
Organizations should establish transparency policies documenting the origin and history of training and generated data.
Organizations should evaluate risk-relevant capabilities and safety-measure robustness before deployment and on an ongoing basis.
Risk tiers should consider information integrity, dependencies, public safety, harmful output, psychological impacts, misuse, security vulnerabilities, group impacts, and reliability.
Organizations should devise a plan to halt development or deployment when a system poses unacceptable negative risk.
Periodic review should cover content provenance, incident monitoring, after-action review, incident disclosure, and retention of TEVV history.
Inventory entries should include provenance, known issues, human oversight, rights and data considerations, and underlying models and versions.
Decommissioning should consider deactivation, data retention and security, leakage, dependencies, open-source components, and user emotional entanglement.
Organizations should define roles, policies, and procedures to communicate incidents and performance to AI actors and affected downstream stakeholders.
Organizations should deploy and document fact-checking techniques, especially for information from multiple or unknown sources.
Organizations should develop and implement tests to identify synthetic GAI content that may be indistinguishable from human-generated content.
Organizations should perform diligence on training-data use and establish policies for curation, use, storage, and protection of third-party IP and sensitive data.
The summary should identify the AI RMF companion purpose, GAI risks, and actions organized around governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing, and incident disclosure.
The primary considerations are governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing, and incident disclosure, and they inform risk-management actions.

The Transformer is an attention-only sequence-transduction architecture that dispenses with recurrence and convolutions.
Sequential dependence on previous hidden states prevents parallelization within training examples.
Self-attention relates positions in a single sequence to compute its representation.
Scaled dot-product attention takes query-key dot products, divides by the square root of the key dimension, and applies softmax to produce value weights.
Multi-head attention uses multiple learned projections of queries, keys, and values and applies attention in parallel.
Positional encodings inject relative or absolute token-position information because the model has no recurrence or convolution.
